newsitem.title: CHINA: FEATURE - Is Hong Kong model for Shanghai boom?.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - Is Hong Kong model for Shanghai boom?.

text.p: Shanghai is China's financial hub, but that position of pride will disappear on July 1 when the booming British colony of Hong Kong returns to the Chinese fold.

The humming metropolis that was once known as the "Paris of the East" -- and is now dubbed China's dragonhead -- is undeterred, and officials are seizing on Hong Kong as a model to duplicate and then to surpass.
Are the two cities bitter rivals or friendly competitors for the title of China's financial champion?
Some officials have tried to play down the rivalry in recent months -- but for Shanghainese, pride clearly wants to win.

"Now the country wants to develop Shanghai as an international finance and trade centre, and a top international metropolis," said the city's chief engineer for urban planning, Chen Youhua, whose task is to make the vision a reality.
Officials have said that Shanghai wants to be established as the biggest financial centre in China by the end of the century, the biggest in the region by 2005 and a global financial centre by 2010.

Shanghai envies Hong Kong, which reverts to Chinese sovereignty at midnight on June 30, for its ascendancy, but officials realise their city cannot develop without Hong Kong's capital and expertise, business executives and analysts said.
"Shanghai was once one of the leading cities in the world," said Stephen Yuen, president of the Hong Kong Institute of Real Estate Administration, which has advised Shanghai on planning.
"They have a strong desire to learn from other people and, at the same time, surpass other cities," he said.
Duplicating Hong Kong will not be easy.

The Chinese city's legal system is not as predictable or transparent as Hong Kong's, the cellular phone system doesn't work properly, the tax system is confusing and the bureaucracy slow, foreign business executives said.

Shanghai's foreign currency B share market lacks the liquidity and large flotations by individual companies that appeal to major international fund managers who are scurrying to invest in Hong Kong's bourse, brokers said.
The Chinese city also is missing other crucial ingredients of Hong Kong's success -- the rule of law and autonomous decision-making power, analysts said.
"In Hong Kong, you know nothing can go seriously wrong with the British government behind everything -- that makes a big difference," said a Hong Kong lawyer based in Shanghai.
"The people are predominantly Chinese, but you do business the Western way and get rich the Western way," he said. "These are the elements which make Hong Kong great."
Chinese officials are aware of some of the reasons for Hong Kong's success -- a service-based economy, a free port, free capital flows, and efficiency in getting things done.
For Shanghai to advance, it must first fully take to heart the concept of quality of service, which has become second nature to the work force in Hong Kong, analysts said.
The service industry now accounts for only 42 percent of Shanghai's gross domestic product, while in Hong Kong the figure is almost double that, Chinese officials said.
Shanghai also lacks the air and shipping links that made Hong Kong an economic powerhouse. Hong Kong's port moved 13.3 million standard containers in 1996, compared with 1.79 million for Shanghai.
The world's largest banks flock to Hong Kong, but in Shanghai, only nine foreign banks have so far been allowed to conduct business in the local yuan currency.
Shanghai will be able to match many elements of Hong Kong in 10-15 years, but simply copying Hong Kong's skyline will not be enough.

"Shanghai wants to be like Hong Kong," said John Crossman, Shanghai representative for Jardine Fleming Securities. "But Shanghai officials don't realise the pretty buildings in Hong Kong didn't come first.
"Shanghai has to hollow out its industrial base, polish up the ports and make itself into a service centre for the Yangtze River valley," he said.

After such improvements, Shanghai will draw the foreign shipping firms, insurance companies and financial institutions that are the hallmarks of a service-based economy -- and among the strengths of Hong Kong.
The business climate will improve with time, but analysts warn that Shanghai's development may ultimately be restricted by central government control.

"The legal system in Shanghai is getting better for foreign companies, but I don't think Shanghai will be given the power to legislate on its own without the blessing of Beijing," said the Hong Kong lawyer.
